newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Saved UBS files could aid Swiss war probe.
newsitem.headline: Saved UBS files could aid Swiss war probe.

text.p: Old documents saved by a watchman from shredding at Switzerland's biggest bank could help a sweeping probe of the Swiss financial role in World War Two, the historical commission behind the probe said on Thursday.

The commission's finding confirmed that the pre-1945 records rescued from Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) were relevant to the sweeping review of Swiss wartime financial ties, which had been uncertain since the case came up in January.
Nightwatchman Christopher Mieli rescued the records from carts marked for shredding and gave them to a Zurich Jewish group, which publicly handed the files to prosecutors.
"From our preliminary review of the documents, we have concluded that parts of them could be useful for the commission's work," commission chief of staff Linus von Castelnur told Reuters.

Castelnur confirmed a report in the Swiss tabloid Blick that the independent commission of Swiss and foreign historians appointed by the Swiss government had told prosecutors the documents came under federal protection from destruction.
"We consider some parts of the papers to be relevant and useful, as stated in the federal decree," he said, referring to a December government order setting up the commission.
The decree prohibited destruction of any potentially helpful records.

The UBS records were from a subsidiary bought by the bank in 1945, including loans made in Germany in the 1920s and 1930s. UBS at the time called the act a "regrettable accident" but said no client records were lost that could assist the search for any dormant accounts of Holocaust victims.

The commission was formed in December to draw up a comprehensive history of Switzerland's role as neutral banker to Nazis as well as victims of the Holocaust and the flow of assets from both sides before, during and after the war.

Castelnur said a researcher had finally looked at the UBS papers in late May. The commission then wrote to Zurich prosecutors in early June to say the documents fell under the scope of the federal decree.
No comment was immediately available from Zurich prosecutors, who are investigating whether UBS broke the law on document protection and whether Meili violated bank secrecy laws.

Meili was fired and has since fled to the United States, where Congress has praised him as a hero and voted to let him immigrate with his wife Giuseppina and two young children. President Bill Clinton must still sign the motion.
